description: We are enthusiastic students passionate about technology, space science, AI, and software development. We aim to participate in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and build an innovative solution using NASA’s open data. We value creativity, teamwork, problem-solving, and learning, and welcome members skilled in AI/ML, coding, web development, data analysis, design, and communication.
summary:
EarthScore is a web app that lets anyone hear Earth data. You pick any point on an interactive 3D globe, and the app fetches ten years (2016–2025) of monthly NASA data live. Each month becomes one musical note: higher pitch means a higher value. Five data streams can be played: NASA POWER air temperature, rainfall and aerosol optical depth (haze), plus NOAA global CO₂ and methane. The chart, timeline and globe move in sync with the sound. Regional Compare plays two places one after the other in stereo (A in the left ear, B in the right), so contrasts such as Kolkata vs Svalbard can be heard at once. A DAW Engine exports any sonification as a WAV file for classrooms and presentations.
This answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by giving people a second way to understand our planet. Long time series are hard to read for non-experts and inaccessible for people with low vision; sound makes seasons, extremes and differences between places easy to notice. Every note comes from a real, validated measurement, and missing data stays silent instead of being invented.
details:
What it does

EarthScore turns real Earth observation data into sound. In the Planetary Explorer, the user picks a point on a 3D globe: a preset (Kolkata, Svalbard, Amazon, Tokyo, Sahara, Tuvalu), a searched place, or coordinates. The app downloads ten years of monthly data (2016–2025) directly in the browser and plays it as music, one note per month. A fixed mapping turns each value into a pitch between 220 Hz and 880 Hz (two octaves). The same value always gives the same note, in every place and every year, so places and years can be compared fairly.

Five sound sources

•       Temperature – NASA POWER T2M, air temperature at 2 m (°C)

•       Rainfall – NASA POWER PRECTOTCORR, bias-corrected precipitation (mm/day)

•       Air quality – NASA POWER AOD_55, aerosol optical depth: how much dust, smoke and haze dims sunlight (a proxy for particle pollution, not an official air-quality index)

•       CO₂ and methane – NOAA global monthly means, clearly labelled as worldwide values

How it works

One shared playback controller schedules every note on the Web Audio clock. The timeline, month cards, chart marker and globe badge follow exactly what is being heard. Users can play the whole decade or one year, pause, resume, stop, seek by year or by clicking the chart, change speed (0.5×, 1×, 2×), and set the volume or mute.

Regional Compare aligns two locations month by month on one chart with a shared scale and shows the values and their difference (A − B). Playback alternates A then B with the same mapping; with headphones A is heard on the left and B on the right.

The DAW Engine renders any sonification, including the stereo comparison, to a WAV file that can be scrubbed and downloaded.

Side panels show current weather, air-quality pollutants, rainfall history, MODIS vegetation index (NDVI), greenhouse gases and population, each labelled with its real source.

Benefits and intended impact

•       Accessibility: a second, non-visual way to explore climate data, useful for people with low vision and for anyone who finds graphs hard to read.

•       Education: teachers and students can hear seasons, monsoons, polar cold and polluted months, and compare places side by side.

•       Outreach: audio files can be shared in classrooms, talks and museums.

•       Trust: the app always shows where each value comes from and what it does not claim.

Creativity

Instead of adding sound effects to a chart, EarthScore makes the data itself the music. Stereo panning turns comparison into a spatial listening experience. The same pitch scale is used for every place, so the ear can judge differences directly.

Factors we considered

•       Scientific honesty: NASA fill values (−999) and missing months are kept as missing and stay silent; they are never shown as zero. Implausible values and wrong units are rejected.

•       Reliability: a 15-second timeout, with saved real NASA data for the preset locations if the API is down (the app tells the user).

•       Synchronisation: notes are scheduled on the audio clock so sound and visuals never drift apart.

•       Usability: keyboard control, mute, speed control, and a layout that works on phones.

•       Transparency: a Data Sources & Methodology page explains each source, the pitch formula and the limitations (it does not detect heatwaves or prove climate trends).

Tools and languages

TypeScript, React, Vite, react-globe.gl / three.js (3D globe), Recharts (charts), Tone.js and the Web Audio API (sound and WAV rendering), Vitest (183 automated tests), Playwright (browser checks), GitHub and GitHub Codespaces (development), Vercel (hosting). No backend and no API keys are needed.

Use of AI (Super Intelligence) tools

We used an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) to help write and review code, tests and documentation, and to help draft this project text. The team chose the challenge, the design, the data sources and the sound mapping, and ran, tested and verified everything. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used: all sound is generated live from the data, and the globe uses NASA Blue Marble imagery.
